title: Deep in one: the Gospel of John
for: I want to know John's Gospel well
subtitle: Twelve sessions through all twenty-one chapters of John: the Word made flesh, the signs, the long evening before the cross, and the risen Lord at a fire by the sea.
intro: This track reads the Gospel of John slowly, a chapter or two at a sitting, twelve sessions in all. John tells the same story as Matthew, Mark and Luke, from John the Baptist to the empty tomb, but from a different height. It begins before creation, spends five chapters on a single evening, and says openly why it was written: so that the reader may believe and have life.

Each session takes about fifteen minutes. Read the chapter, then its notes in plain words, then come back to one question, one thing to do and one verse to keep. John's vocabulary is small, light and life, truth and love, believing and remaining, and the same words return deeper each time. Watch for them. Each session ends with a guide for a group.

about: This guide is for anyone leading a small group through Deep in one: the Gospel of John. The group meets twelve times and reads all twenty-one chapters, one or two at a meeting. John suits a mixed group well. Many people have come to faith by reading it first, and no one has reached the bottom of it, so the new reader and the long-time believer can sit at the same table and both be stretched.

Each person reads the chapters, their notes and the session before the group meets. The meeting reads part of the text aloud and talks it over, using the group guide for that session, which is gathered below in order with the page each session opens and the question it asks.

sections.title: The group
body: Four to ten people is a good size, small enough that everyone speaks. Meet for about seventy-five minutes, once a week, for twelve meetings, and keep the end time you promised. A leader doesn't need to be a scholar. A leader needs to have read the chapters and their notes, and to be willing to say plainly when they don't know.

sections.title: The room
body: Sit where everyone can see each other, with the text open in front of everyone, in print or on a phone. John's long conversations read well aloud in parts, so let different voices take Jesus, Nicodemus, the woman at the well or Pilate. Make it plain at the first meeting that anyone may pass on any question, that what people say about their own lives stays in the room, and that no one has to pray aloud.

sections.title: The order of a meeting
body: About seventy-five minutes, in this order. Keep to the times loosely and to the end time strictly.
steps: Ten minutes: the opening question, once round the circle. Anyone may pass.
Fifteen minutes: read the heart of the chapters aloud, in parts where there is a conversation, while the others follow.
Thirty-five minutes: the three questions to talk over, in order. Ask where each answer is in the text.
Five minutes: one person reads the verse to keep, and the group says what it noticed in it.
Five minutes: the prayer prompt, in your own words.
Five minutes: name the next chapters and the page the next session opens, and say when you will meet.

sections.title: When a hard question comes
body: John raises hard questions of its own: how it differs from the other three Gospels, a story the oldest manuscripts don't contain, words about eating his flesh that churches read in different ways, and the way it speaks of the Jews. When the group reaches one, read the note on it together before anyone answers. Where Christians read a passage in more than one way, give each reading its strongest form and don't settle for the group what the church has not settled.

Some questions are about whether any of it is true. Welcome them. Thomas asks for evidence in chapter 20, and Jesus meets him instead of scolding him. The Honest Answers and the case for the faith on this site take many such questions up, and the sessions link several. If no one knows, write the question down and bring it back the next week.

sections.title: When someone is hurting
body: John is full of people at the end of themselves: a man ill for thirty-eight years, a man blind from birth whose neighbours ask whose sin caused it, two sisters at a brother's tomb, a friend who denied Jesus three times. Their stories will touch someone's own. When that happens, stop and listen. Thank the person for saying it, don't explain their suffering for them, and don't hurry them back to the passage. Jesus wept at a grave he was about to open.

Some passages have been misused to wound. Words about the Jews have been read as contempt for the Jewish people, though Jesus, his mother and every disciple in the book were Jews; the notes refuse that reading, and so should the group. If someone says that anyone is harming them or a child, take it seriously and don't promise to keep it secret.

sections.title: When to point someone to Find Help
body: Point someone to Find Help when what they carry has become too heavy to set down: grief that has taken their sleep or appetite for weeks, fear or guilt that will not let them rest, harm done to them at home or in a church, or any sign that they no longer want to be alive. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn, and its lines for help right now are open day and night. If anyone is in danger now, call your local emergency number. A leader is a friend in that moment, not a counsellor, and the kindest thing is often to stay with the person while they make the first call.

sessions.title: The Word became flesh
teaching: Mark begins at a river and Matthew with a family tree. John goes back further than both, to the first words of Genesis: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1). The Word is with God, so he is distinct, and is God, so he is not less. Then comes the sentence the whole book hangs on: “The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us” (John 1:14). The verb for dwelling recalls the tent where God's glory lived among Israel in the wilderness.

The church spent three centuries learning to say what this chapter says, and at Nicaea in 325 it confessed the Son to be of one being with the Father. The rest of the chapter comes down to earth. A voice in the wilderness points away from himself to the Lamb of God. Two men follow Jesus and he asks what they want. The answer that runs through the chapter is an invitation, not an argument: come and see.

open.label: John 1, passage by passage
open.why: The prologue, John the Baptist's witness and the first disciples, each passage explained in plain words, with what its first hearers would have heard.

also.label: John's introduction in the Study Bible
also.why: Who wrote John, when and for whom, how the book is built around signs and one long evening, and how to read it.

also.label: The Gospel of John
also.why: The whole book in short pictures, so you can see its shape before you read it slowly.

also.label: The Nicene Creed
also.why: The creed of 325 and 381, with notes, which puts John's first chapter into the words the churches still confess together.

sessions.question: John says no one has ever seen God, but the Son has made him known. What do you expect to learn about God by watching Jesus?
sessions.do: Read the whole of John 1:1-18 aloud twice. The second time, mark every word that comes back from Genesis 1, and every word that John will use again later: light, life, glory, truth.

verse.text: The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us. We have seen His glory, the glory of the one and only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth.

group.open: What is a book, film or song whose opening told you what kind of thing it was going to be?
discuss: John opens with the same words as Genesis. What is he claiming by starting there rather than with a birth or a baptism?
John the Baptist keeps saying who he is not. Why might that be the right posture for anyone who points to Jesus?
Jesus answers the first disciples with come and see. What would that invitation look like if someone in your life asked you about him?
group.pray: Give thanks that God has made himself known in a person and not only in words, and ask that each person in the group would come and see over the coming weeks.

sessions.title: New wine, a new temple, a new birth
teaching: Chapters 2 and 3 set three old things side by side with three new ones. At a wedding in Cana the wine runs out, a shame for the host, and Jesus fills six stone jars kept for Jewish washing with wine better than the first. John calls it the first of his signs: a miracle that points past itself. Then Jesus drives the traders out of the temple and says, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up again” (John 2:19). John adds that he meant his body. The place where God meets his people is about to become a person.

Matthew, Mark and Luke place the clearing of the temple in the last week, and John places it at the start. Some readers think it happened twice; others think John set it first on purpose, as a key to the whole book. Then Nicodemus comes by night, a teacher of Israel, and Jesus tells him he must be born again, or from above, for the Greek word means both. Nicodemus hears only the first sense, and the conversation turns on the second.

open.label: John 3, passage by passage
open.why: Nicodemus at night, the snake lifted up in the wilderness, God so loved the world, and John the Baptist stepping aside, each explained plainly.

also.label: John 2, passage by passage
also.why: The wine at Cana and the clearing of the temple, with what the stone jars and the temple meant to the people who saw them.

also.label: John 3:16
also.why: The best-known verse in the Bible taken slowly, phrase by phrase, back inside the night conversation where Jesus first said it.

also.label: New birth in the Study Bible
also.why: What the whole Bible says about being born from above, from Ezekiel's new heart to Nicodemus, and how the churches have understood it.

sessions.question: Nicodemus came at night with a respectful compliment, and Jesus answered with a demand he could not meet himself. Why do you think Jesus answered that way?
sessions.do: Read John 3:1-21 as one conversation, and stop where Nicodemus stops speaking. Write down what you think he took home with him that night. Then look ahead to 19:39 to see where he turns up again.

verse.text: For God so loved the world that He gave His one and only Son, that everyone who believes in Him shall not perish but have eternal life.

care: Sometimes guilt that will not lift needs more than a Bible verse. It can be part of anxiety, depression or a habit of the mind that keeps returning to the same fear. That is not a failure of faith. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor or a doctor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: Have you ever had a conversation late at night that changed how you saw something?
discuss: Jesus' first sign saves a family from embarrassment at a wedding. What does it say about him that he began there?
Jesus calls his own body the temple. What changes if the place to meet God is a person rather than a building?
Nicodemus knew a great deal and still did not understand. What keeps learned people, or religious people, from hearing what Jesus says?
group.pray: Give thanks that God so loved the world, and pray for anyone you know who, like Nicodemus, is asking questions quietly and at a distance.

sessions.title: Living water, and a man by a pool
teaching: Nicodemus came by night, a respected teacher and a man of Israel. The next conversation is the reverse at every point. Jesus, tired and thirsty, sits at a well in Samaria at noon and asks a Samaritan woman for a drink. Jews and Samaritans did not share vessels, and teachers did not talk alone with women. The text never calls her wicked; a woman in her world could be widowed or sent away more than once with no say in it. Jesus offers her living water, she becomes the first in the book to carry his name to a whole town, and the town calls him “the Savior of the world” (John 4:42).

Chapter 5 brings another long-suffering person, a man ill for thirty-eight years beside a pool in Jerusalem. Jesus heals him on the Sabbath and is accused of breaking it, and then of something larger, calling God his own Father and making himself equal with God. Jesus doesn't deny the charge. He says the Son does what he sees the Father doing.

open.label: John 4, passage by passage
open.why: The well at noon, the living water, worship in spirit and truth, and the official's son, each explained with what its first hearers knew about Samaria.

also.label: John 5, passage by passage
also.why: The man by the pool, the Sabbath argument, and Jesus' long answer about the Father, the Son and the witnesses to him.

also.label: The Bible atlas
also.why: Find Samaria between Judea and Galilee, and see why a Jewish traveller going north had to choose whether to pass through it.

sessions.question: The woman tried to turn the conversation to an old argument about where to worship. When does talking about religion become a way of keeping God at a distance?
sessions.do: Read John 4:1-42 and count how many times the woman speaks, and how her name for Jesus changes as she does: a Jew, sir, a prophet, the Christ. Write down where you are on that list.

verse.text: But whoever drinks the water I give him will never thirst. Indeed, the water I give him will become in him a fount of water springing up to eternal life.

group.open: Who are the people your own community finds hardest to sit down and talk with?
discuss: Jesus asks the woman for help before he offers her anything. Why might he begin as the one in need?
Jesus says true worshippers will worship in spirit and in truth, not on a mountain or in a city. What does that leave out, and what does it leave in?
The man by the pool is asked if he wants to be well, and answers with a complaint. What do you make of that question?
group.pray: Pray for someone you have kept at a distance, and give thanks that Jesus went through Samaria on purpose.

sessions.title: The bread of life
teaching: Chapter 6 begins with five thousand fed near Passover, the one sign all four Gospels record, and the crowd wants to make Jesus king by force. He withdraws. The next day they find him and ask for more bread, the way their ancestors had manna in the wilderness. Jesus says the true bread from heaven is not a meal but a person: “I am the bread of life” (John 6:35). The crowd that wanted a king starts to grumble, like Israel in the desert.

Then he goes further, saying that whoever eats his flesh and drinks his blood has eternal life. Christians read these words in different ways. Catholic and Orthodox Christians hear in them the Lord's Supper, where Christ gives himself truly. Lutheran and Reformed readers also hear the Supper here, while understanding his presence in it differently. Many other Protestants read the chapter mainly as a picture of believing, since Jesus says coming to him and believing in him satisfy hunger and thirst. Each reading holds to Christ as the one life comes from, and the notes set them out without choosing.

open.label: John 6, passage by passage
open.why: The crowd fed, Jesus on the water, the bread from heaven and the hard saying, with how the churches have read it set out fairly.

also.label: The calendar and festivals of Israel
also.why: John sets his story by the feasts, Passover, Booths and Dedication, and this guide says what each one remembered and how it was kept.

also.label: Baptism and the Lord's Supper
also.why: What Scripture says about the Supper and how the traditions read it, so you can weigh John 6 with the rest of the Bible open.

sessions.question: Many disciples left when the teaching became hard, and Peter stayed because there was nowhere else to go. Is that a weak reason to stay, or a strong one?
sessions.do: Read John 6:60-71 slowly, then write down one thing in what you believe that you find hard to accept, and one reason you have not walked away from it.

verse.text: Simon Peter replied, “Lord, to whom would we go? You have the words of eternal life.”

group.open: What is a meal you still remember, and what made it more than food?
discuss: The crowd wanted to make Jesus king after they had eaten. Why did he refuse a following built on full stomachs?
Christians read the words about eating his flesh in different ways. What do the readings share, even where they differ?
Jesus asks the twelve whether they want to leave too. Why do you think he gave them the choice?
group.pray: Give thanks for daily bread and for the bread of life, and pray for anyone in the group for whom the teaching has become hard.

sessions.title: The light of the world
teaching: Chapters 7 and 8 take place at the Feast of Booths, when Jerusalem remembered the wilderness years. Jewish sources describe water poured out at the altar and great lamps lit in the temple courts during the feast. On its last day Jesus stands and calls the thirsty to come to him and drink, and soon after he says, “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12). The crowd divides. Some say he is a good man, some that he deceives the people, and the guards sent to arrest him come back saying no one ever spoke like this.

The story of the woman caught in adultery (7:53 to 8:11) is not in the oldest manuscripts, and many scholars think it a true story the church kept and later set here; the notes give the evidence. The argument that follows climbs until Jesus says, “Before Abraham was born, I am” (John 8:58), taking the name God gave Moses at the bush. They pick up stones, which shows they understood him.

open.label: John 8, passage by passage
open.why: The woman brought to Jesus, the light of the world, the truth that sets free and the words before Abraham, each explained plainly.

also.label: John 7, passage by passage
also.why: Jesus' brothers, the whispering crowds at the feast and the rivers of living water, with what the feast meant to those who kept it.

also.label: Passages not in the earliest Bibles
also.why: The woman caught in adultery and the other famous passages missing from the oldest copies, with the evidence on both sides and what it means.

also.label: Did Jesus claim to be God?
also.why: The strongest case that the claim was added later, and the reasons to think it reaches back to Jesus himself.

sessions.question: The crowd split into those who called him good, a deceiver, or something more. Which of those answers have you given, and which do you give now?
sessions.do: Read John 8:31-36 and write down what Jesus says freedom is, and what he says slavery is. Name one thing that has a hold on you that you would not call slavery out loud.

verse.text: Once again, Jesus spoke to the people and said, “I am the light of the world. Whoever follows Me will never walk in the darkness, but will have the light of life.”

care: If you are being hurt, at home, at work or in a church, tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: When have you been in real darkness, a power cut or a night outdoors, and what was it like when the light came?
discuss: The story of the woman is missing from the oldest copies, yet churches still read it. What do you make of how Christians have handled that?
Jesus says the truth will make you free, and his hearers say they have never been slaves. Why is that so hard to admit?
They picked up stones when he said before Abraham, I am. What does that tell you about what they heard him claim?
group.pray: Ask for light where each of you is in the dark, and give thanks that the one who claimed God's name also refused to condemn the woman brought to him.

sessions.title: The man born blind and the good shepherd
teaching: The disciples see a man blind from birth and ask, “Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?” (John 9:2). Jesus refuses the question's frame. Neither, he says, and he makes mud, sends the man to wash, and the man sees. Then the chapter becomes a trial in which everyone is questioned except Jesus: the neighbours, the parents, who are too frightened of being put out of the synagogue to speak, and the man himself, who grows bolder each time. His witness is the plainest in the book: he was blind and now he sees. They throw him out, and Jesus finds him.

Chapter 10 follows without a break. The leaders who threw out a sheep are set beside a shepherd who knows his sheep by name and lays down his life for them. Israel's prophets had already charged their leaders as false shepherds and promised that God himself would shepherd his flock, and Jesus steps into that promise.

open.label: John 9, passage by passage
open.why: The question of who sinned, the healing, the trial of a man who can now see, and who is truly blind, each explained plainly.

also.label: John 10, passage by passage
also.why: The shepherd and the gate, no one snatching the sheep from his hand, and the words at the Feast of Dedication, explained plainly.

also.label: If God is good, why is there so much suffering?
also.why: The disciples wanted a cause for a man's blindness. This answer takes the larger question seriously without handing anyone a cheap reason.

also.label: Pray Psalm 23
also.why: The shepherd psalm Jesus' hearers knew by heart, prayed slowly a line at a time, beside the good shepherd who says he is that shepherd.

sessions.question: The disciples looked at a suffering man and asked whose fault it was. Whose suffering do you explain to yourself so that you don't have to stop?
sessions.do: Read John 9 and make two short lists: everyone who asks a question, and everyone who answers one. Notice who is the only person in the chapter who never changes his story.

verse.text: I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down His life for the sheep.

care: It needs to be said plainly. The Bible does not teach that sickness comes from too little faith, or that a person who stays ill did not believe enough. Paul prayed and was not healed, and no one blames him. If you live with chronic illness, pain or disability, you are not a failure of faith. Your worth to God does not rise or fall with your body. If the weight of it is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a doctor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

If you have been harmed by a controlling leader or church, what was done was wrong, and it was not your fault. Being taken in by someone who seemed godly is not a sign of weak faith. You are free to step away and to tell someone you trust. If you were abused in other ways, or a crime was done, it should be reported to the authorities. A pastor or counsellor outside that church may help you sort out what happened. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: What is one thing you know for certain, even if you can't explain how you know it?
discuss: Jesus refuses to say whose sin caused the blindness. What does that refusal free the man, and us, from?
The parents were afraid of being put out and said nothing. When has fear of losing your place kept you quiet?
Jesus contrasts the shepherd with hired hands who run. What marks the difference between them in a church today?
group.pray: Pray for anyone who has been put out, by a church or a family, and give thanks that Jesus went looking for the man after they threw him out.

sessions.title: Lazarus, and the hour comes
teaching: Jesus hears that Lazarus, whom he loves, is ill, and he stays where he is two more days. By the time he reaches Bethany his friend has been in the tomb four days. Martha meets him on the road with faith and grief together, and he tells her, “I am the resurrection and the life” (John 11:25). Mary falls at his feet saying the same words her sister said, and he is deeply moved and weeps. The one about to raise the dead still stops to grieve. Then he calls Lazarus out, and the dead man comes.

The greatest sign is the one that gets Jesus killed. The council meets, and the high priest says it is better for one man to die for the people than for the nation to perish, saying more than he knows. In chapter 12 Mary pours perfume on Jesus' feet, the crowds wave branches, some Greeks ask to see him, and Jesus says the hour has come. A grain of wheat must fall into the earth and die before it bears fruit.

open.label: John 11, passage by passage
open.why: The delay, Martha and Mary, Jesus weeping, Lazarus called out, and the council's decision, each passage explained in plain words.

also.label: John 12, passage by passage
also.why: Mary's perfume, the king on a donkey, the grain of wheat and the end of Jesus' public teaching, explained plainly.

also.label: Resurrection in the Study Bible
also.why: What the whole Bible hopes for when it speaks of the dead rising, from the prophets to Martha's faith on the road to Bethany.

sessions.question: Jesus wept at a tomb he was about to open. What does that tell you about how God regards your grief?
sessions.do: Read John 11:17-37 slowly and notice that Martha and Mary say the same sentence to Jesus and he answers each one differently. Write down which answer you need this week.

verse.text: Jesus said to her, “I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in Me will live, even though he dies.”

care: Grief is not a lack of faith. If your grief is so heavy that you cannot carry it, please tell someone: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: Who taught you how to grieve, by word or by example?
discuss: Jesus loved this family and still waited two days. How do you hold that delay together with his love?
Martha says she believes and in the same breath says if only you had been here. Can both be true at once?
Raising Lazarus is what finally decides the council against Jesus. What does it mean that giving life cost him his?
group.pray: Name before God, if you are willing, someone you have lost, and give thanks that Jesus weeps with those who weep and calls the dead by name.

sessions.title: Feet washed, and the way to the Father
teaching: From chapter 13 John slows almost to a stop. Five chapters are given to one evening. Jesus knows he has come from God and is going to God, and so, John says, he takes off his outer garment and washes his disciples' feet, the work of a household's lowest servant. Peter refuses and then asks for a bath. Judas is washed too, and goes out, and John writes that it was night. Then Jesus gives a new commandment, to love one another as he has loved them, and tells Peter he will deny him three times before morning.

Chapter 14 answers troubled hearts. There are many rooms in the Father's house, Jesus says, and Thomas asks how they can know the way. The answer is a person: “I am the way and the truth and the life” (John 14:6). Philip asks to see the Father, and Jesus says whoever has seen him has seen the Father. He promises another Advocate, the Spirit of truth, who will be with them for ever.

open.label: John 13, passage by passage
open.why: The footwashing, the example, the betrayer, the new commandment and the warning to Peter, each explained in plain words.

also.label: John 14, passage by passage
also.why: The Father's house, the way and the truth and the life, the promise of the Spirit and the peace the world cannot give.

also.label: Is Jesus the only way?
also.why: The hardest sentence in this chapter for a modern reader, taken seriously, with the objection given its full strength before any answer.

also.label: The Holy Spirit in the Study Bible
also.why: What Scripture says about the Spirit, from creation to Pentecost, and the Advocate Jesus promises on this last evening.

sessions.question: Peter would rather do anything for Jesus than let Jesus wash his feet. Why is it so hard to be served?
sessions.do: This week, do one task for someone that is beneath what you think of as your place, without mentioning it to anyone. Then read John 13:1-17 again and notice what Jesus knew before he knelt.

verse.text: A new commandment I give you: Love one another. As I have loved you, so you also must love one another.

care: This passage is not a rebuke of people who live with an anxiety disorder, panic attacks or depression. Those are real illnesses of body and mind, and they need care, not blame. Getting help is not a lack of faith, and nothing in this verse forbids it. A doctor, a counselor, medicine, one trusted person who will stay can all be part of how God cares for you. The Honest Answer ‘Is my anxiety a spiritual failure?’ says more. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: What is the humblest job you have ever done, and how did people treat you while you did it?
discuss: Jesus washed Judas's feet knowing what he would do. What does that do to your idea of whom love is owed to?
Thomas asks for a map and Jesus gives him a person. Why is that answer both a comfort and an offence?
Jesus says the world will know his disciples by their love for one another. What would someone conclude from watching your church?
group.pray: Pray for the humility to be served and to serve, and pray by name for anyone in the group whose heart is troubled this week.

sessions.title: The vine, the Spirit and the prayer
teaching: The prophets had pictured Israel as God's vine, planted with care and too often fruitless. Jesus says, “I am the true vine” (John 15:1), and the word that carries chapter 15 is remain. A branch does not strain to produce grapes; it stays joined and the life comes through. Then he calls them friends, warns that the world will hate them as it hated him, and in chapter 16 says it is better that he go, because the Spirit will come, convict the world and guide them into all truth. Their grief will turn to joy, like a mother's after birth.

Chapter 17 is the prayer that ends the evening, long called his high priestly prayer. Jesus prays for himself, for the eleven, and then for everyone who will believe through their word, which includes every later reader of the book. He asks that they may be one, as he and the Father are one, so that the world may believe. A church divided for centuries reads that line and is judged by it.

open.label: John 15, passage by passage
open.why: The true vine, remaining, friends rather than servants, and the world's hatred, each passage explained plainly.

also.label: John 16, passage by passage
also.why: Why it is good that Jesus goes, the Spirit who guides into truth, and grief turned to joy, explained plainly.

also.label: Study John 17 step by step
also.why: The guided walk takes you through the prayer in seven steps, so you notice what Jesus asks and for whom before you read about it.

also.label: The Trinity
also.why: The Father, the Son and the Spirit speak and act together all through these chapters. This page sets out what the church confesses about them.

sessions.question: Jesus prayed for people who would believe through the disciples' word, which means he prayed for you. What do you make of that?
sessions.do: Read John 17:20-26 aloud and put your own name, and then the name of a Christian you disagree with, where the prayer speaks of those who will believe. Notice what Jesus asks for both of you.

verse.text: I am the vine and you are the branches. The one who remains in Me, and I in him, will bear much fruit. For apart from Me you can do nothing.

care: If you have been harmed by someone in a church, and were told to forgive and say nothing, what happened to you may have been wrong. Please talk with someone you trust outside that situation. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: Who is a friend you have stayed close to for many years, and what has kept you close?
discuss: A branch bears fruit by remaining, not by straining. Where are you straining at what only remaining can give?
Jesus says it is better for them that he goes away. What did they gain by losing his visible presence?
Jesus prays that his followers may be one so that the world may believe. What does our division say to the world?
group.pray: Pray for the church in your town by name, beyond your own congregation, and ask that Christians who disagree would be one as Jesus prayed.

sessions.title: The arrest, the trial and the cross
teaching: In John's telling Jesus is never a victim swept along. In the garden he steps forward and asks whom they are seeking, and when he says “I am He” (John 18:5) the soldiers fall back to the ground. Inside the high priest's house he speaks openly, while outside at a charcoal fire Peter denies him three times. Before Pilate the questions turn around. Pilate asks if he is a king; Jesus says he came to testify to the truth; Pilate asks what truth is, and walks out before an answer.

John dates the crucifixion to the day of preparation for Passover, the afternoon the lambs were killed, and the other Gospels appear to place the Last Supper on Passover itself; scholars weigh several ways the accounts may fit. On the cross Jesus gives his mother to the beloved disciple, says he thirsts, and then, “It is finished” (John 19:30). The word means a work completed. Nicodemus, who first came by night, now comes in daylight with spices for his burial.

open.label: John 19, passage by passage
open.why: Here is the man, no king but Caesar, the title over the cross, his mother, it is finished and the burial, each explained plainly.

also.label: John 18, passage by passage
also.why: The arrest in the garden, Peter at the fire, and Jesus before Annas and Pilate, with the question of truth.

also.label: The day of the crucifixion
also.why: John and the other Gospels appear to differ on the day. This sets out the problem honestly and the ways scholars have answered it.

also.label: Why crucifixion was so shameful
also.why: What a Roman cross meant to the people who saw one, and why John can still call it the hour of Jesus' glory.

sessions.question: Pilate asked what truth is and did not wait for the answer. What questions do you ask in a way that keeps you from hearing the answer?
sessions.do: Read John 18:15-27 and 21:9 side by side and notice where each charcoal fire burns. Then read 19:25-27 and write down what Jesus does for others while he is dying.

verse.text: When Jesus had received the sour wine, He said, “It is finished.” And bowing His head, He yielded up His spirit.

care: If you feel forsaken right now and the feeling will not lift, please tell someone you trust, a pastor, a friend or a doctor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: When have you watched someone keep their dignity in a situation meant to take it from them?
discuss: In John, Jesus is in command even under arrest. How does that change the way you read his death?
These chapters have been misused to blame the Jewish people for the cross. Why is that reading false to John, who was himself a Jew?
It is finished means a work completed. What work, and what does it leave for anyone else to add?
group.pray: Give thanks in your own words for the cross, and pray for anyone who, like Peter at the fire, has failed Jesus and cannot forget it.

sessions.title: The empty tomb, and Thomas
teaching: Mary Magdalene comes to the tomb while it is still dark and finds the stone moved. Peter and the beloved disciple run, and the grave cloths are lying there, the cloth from his head lying apart. Mary stays weeping and does not know the man she speaks to until he says her name. In all four Gospels women are the first at the empty tomb, in a world where a woman's word counted for little in court, a detail hard to explain as invention. That evening he stands among the locked-in disciples, shows them his hands and side, and breathes on them the Spirit.

Thomas was not there, and he will not believe without touching the wounds. A week later Jesus offers him exactly that, and Thomas answers with the highest confession in the book: “My Lord and my God” (John 20:28). Then John tells the reader why he wrote. The signs were chosen so that you may believe, and believing have life.

open.label: John 20, passage by passage
open.why: The empty tomb, Mary in the garden, the disciples sent, Thomas, and the sentence that says why the book was written.

also.label: Did the resurrection actually happen?
also.why: The question Thomas asked, taken seriously: the strongest objections, the evidence historians weigh, and what follows if it is true.

also.label: The empty tomb
also.why: The historical case for the empty tomb, with the best skeptical alternatives stated fairly and answered on the evidence.

also.label: The resurrection
also.why: Short pictures of what the first witnesses said happened on the third day and why it changed everything they believed.

sessions.question: Jesus did not scold Thomas for wanting evidence, and he still called blessed those who believe without seeing. What would it take for you to say my Lord and my God?
sessions.do: Write down your own honest question about the resurrection, the way Thomas spoke his. Then read the Honest Answer linked here and note one thing it says that you had not considered.

verse.text: But these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in His name.

care: If you are a person whose conscience never rests, who keeps checking whether you have really believed, hear John's words: “Even if our hearts condemn us, God is greater than our hearts, and He knows all things” (1 John 3:20). Such fear can be part of anxiety or a habit of the mind, and that is not a failure of faith. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust, and if the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor or a doctor can help too. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: What is something you refused to believe until you saw it for yourself?
discuss: Mary recognised Jesus when he said her name. Why might John tell the first meeting that way?
Thomas is often called the doubter. Is that fair to him, given what he said a week later?
John says he wrote so that readers may believe. Has the book done that work in you so far, and how?
group.pray: Bring your honest questions to God in your own words, as Thomas did, and give thanks that the risen Jesus came back for the one who was missing.

sessions.title: Breakfast by the sea, and Peter restored
teaching: The book seemed to end at chapter 20, and then it goes on. Seven disciples go fishing on the Sea of Galilee and catch nothing all night. A man on the shore tells them where to cast, the net fills, and the beloved disciple says it is the Lord. Peter jumps into the water. On the beach Jesus has a charcoal fire going with fish and bread on it. John uses that word for a charcoal fire only twice, here and in the courtyard where Peter denied him.

Three times Peter said he did not know him. Now, three times, Jesus asks Peter whether he loves him, and three times gives him work, to feed and tend his sheep. There is no lecture and no probation. Then Jesus tells him how he will die, and Peter turns and asks about the beloved disciple. The answer closes the book on the reader as well as on Peter: “What is that to you? You follow Me” (John 21:22).

open.label: John 21, passage by passage
open.why: The catch at dawn, breakfast on the shore, Peter's three answers, the word about his death and the witness behind the book.

also.label: Is John history or theology?
also.why: Now you have read the whole book, weigh the honest question of how John's portrait relates to what happened, with both sides heard.

also.label: Deep in one: Genesis
also.why: The next track in this program goes back to the first book of the Bible and the beginning that John echoed.

sessions.question: Jesus restored Peter at a fire like the one where he failed. What failure of yours do you think Jesus means to meet you at?
sessions.do: Go back to John 1 this week and read the first chapter again in the light of the last. Write down every word or picture from the end that the beginning already held.

verse.text: Jesus asked a third time, “Simon son of John, do you love Me?” Peter was deeply hurt that Jesus had asked him a third time, “Do you love Me?” “Lord, You know all things,” he replied. “You know I love You.” Jesus said to him, “Feed My sheep.”

care: Sometimes guilt that will not lift needs more than a Bible verse. It can be part of anxiety, depression or a habit of the mind that keeps returning to the same fear. That is not a failure of faith. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor or a doctor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: Which of these twelve sessions will stay with you longest, and why?
discuss: Jesus gives Peter work instead of a lecture. What does that say about how he restores people who have failed?
Peter is told he will die for Jesus, and immediately compares himself with someone else. Why do we do that?
John began with the Word in the beginning and ends with follow me. What lies between those two for you now?
group.pray: Give thanks by name for each person in the group, and ask that each would hear the risen Lord's question to Peter as a question to them.
